title: Preview of Metabolism
objectives: Understand biochemical forms of energy and ATP generation
Recognize redox potential and electron flow in metabolism
Describe major metabolic strategies and phases

overview.title: Pathway Overview
overview.content:
Pathway Overview

Definition & Classification

Metabolism is defined as the sum of all chemical changes in living cells, tissues, and body that results in:

  • Production of energy (ATP)
  • Synthesis of small and large biomolecules
  • Growth and development
  • Elimination of waste material

Classification of Metabolic Pathways

  • Anabolic pathways: Construct macromolecules from simple precursors (e.g., protein synthesis, DNA replication)
  • Catabolic pathways: Break down macromolecules into simple molecules (H2O, CO2, NH4+) to produce energy
  • Amphibolic pathways: Serve dual functions (e.g., citric acid cycle - both energy production and precursor supply)

biochemical_energy.title: Biochemical Energy
biochemical_energy.content:
Biochemical Energy

Energy Carriers

1. ATP (Universal Energy Currency)

  • Formation:
    • Oxidative phosphorylation (mitochondria)
    • Substrate-level phosphorylation
    • Phosphocreatine system (muscle energy shuttle)
    • Adenylate kinase reaction: 2ADP ↔ ATP + AMP
  • Energy Yield:
    • -7.3 kcal/mol per phosphate bond
    • -10.9 kcal/mol for both bonds

2. Other Nucleotides (GTP, UTP, CTP)

  • GTP: Yields GDP + Pi for substrate activation
  • UTP/CTP: Form UDP/CDP-substrate intermediates

3. Coenzyme A (CoA)

  • Derived from pantothenate (vitamin B5)
  • Carries acyl/acetyl groups
  • Essential for fatty acid metabolism

4. Reducing Equivalents

  • NAD, NADP, FAD, FMN
  • Electron carriers for redox reactions
  • Undergo reversible oxidation-reduction

redox.title: Redox Potential
redox.content:
Redox Potential

Electron Flow & Standard Redox Potential

Key Concepts

  • Redox Potential (E°): Measure of electron affinity (volts)
  • Biological Standard: pH 7.0 (H2 potential = -0.42v)
  • Electron Flow: From lower to higher redox potential

Redox Agents

  • Reducing Agents: Negative E° (donate electrons)
  • Oxidizing Agents: Positive E° (accept electrons)

strategies.title: Metabolic Strategies
strategies.content:
Metabolic Strategies

Key Metabolic Strategies

1. Activation of Molecules

  • Phosphorylation/pyrophosphorylation
  • Adenylation
  • CoA binding

2. Enzymatic Catalysis

  • Enables rapid reactions at body temperature
  • Example: Decarboxylation at 37°C vs 200°C required without enzymes

3. Coupled & Sequential Reactions

  • Energy-releasing reactions drive energy-consuming ones
  • Pathway organization maintains favorable thermodynamics

4. Targeted Bond Instability

  • Creates reactive centers in molecules

5. Specialized Carrier Molecules

  • ATP, CoA, NADH, etc.
  • Enable group transfer reactions

clinical.title: Clinical Correlations
clinical.content:
Clinical Correlations

Metabolic Disorders

Energy Metabolism Disorders

  • Phosphocreatine deficiency: Muscle energy impairment
  • CoA deficiency: Fatty acid metabolism disruption

Electron Transport Disorders

  • Mitochondrial diseases affecting ATP production

Enzyme Deficiencies

  • Pyruvate kinase deficiency: Causes hemolytic anemia

faqs.title: FAQs
faqs.content:
FAQs

Q: Why is ATP called the 'universal energy currency'? +

A: Because it's the common intermediate that links energy-producing and energy-consuming processes in all cells, with standardized energy value (~7.3 kcal/mol per phosphate bond).

Q: How does phosphocreatine help muscles? +

A: It acts as an energy reservoir - quickly regenerates ATP during bursts of activity and shuttles mitochondrial ATP to cytosolic sites of use.

Q: What determines electron flow direction? +

A: Electrons always flow from molecules with lower redox potential to those with higher potential.
